title: Namdev

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev, called half-baked by a potter, learned from Visoba Khechar's feet that there's nowhere without God.

Lunch is laid out: a few pieces of flatbread, and a little pot of ghee, clarified butter, to spread on top. Namdev looks away for a moment. A stray dog trots in, snatches the bread, and runs. Namdev jumps up and goes after it. Not with a stick. He's carrying the pot of ghee, calling: wait, that bread is dry, let me butter it for you. That's the story told about him.
screen: `A DOG STEALS THE BREAD.` → `NAMDEV CHASES IT.` → `HE'S CARRYING THE GHEE.`

segments.voice: Visoba taught Namdev that there's no place without God. Here is that lesson trotting off on four legs. Someone who has really learned it can't see a hungry dog as only a thief. In the story, Namdev sees Vitthal in it, and the one problem left is that the bread is dry. Some tellings say Vitthal then shows himself, smiling. Now a harder story. Namdev goes to a temple to sing; tradition places it at Aundha. The priests push him out. In their eyes, a man of his birth doesn't belong there. So Namdev walks around to the back, sits on the ground, and keeps singing. And the story says the temple turned, the whole building swinging around until its door faced Namdev and its back faced the priests. This one Namdev tells himself, in a hymn kept under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs. Roughly, he says he came to the temple laughing and playing, was seized and driven out because of the community he was born into, and the temple turned to face him. So his own words sit inside the Sikh scripture, beside the hymns of the Gurus. Put the two stories side by side. In the first, God is so near that even a dog with stolen lunch is him. In the second, God won't stay in a building that sends his singer away. Both times, God comes around to wherever Namdev already is.
screen: `THE LESSON ON FOUR LEGS.` · `PUSHED OUT OF THE TEMPLE.` · `THE TEMPLE TURNS.` · then, large: `A HYMN IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one creature that annoyed you lately: a neighbor's dog, a pigeon on the sill, someone who took the last cup of coffee. Hold them without the annoyance and ask Namdev's question: if this one were holy too, what would I hand them? Let the answer stay small, just the ghee for the bread, and if you pray, hold them before God.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur who chased a dog to butter its bread, and whose hymn of the turning temple is kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: the butter, not the stick. Even a thief with your lunch can be met with ghee. Day nine hundred eighteen, done.

howItsDone: Varkari devotees in Maharashtra sing Namdev's songs to Vitthal, and Sikhs read and sing the hymns under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib, where his words are kept beside those of the Gurus.

chat.says: Why would Namdev chase a dog with butter instead of a stick?
options: He'd learned there's nowhere without God, so he saw Vitthal even in the dog.
He wanted the dog to drop the bread, so he tried to tempt it with butter.
He thought the dog belonged to the temple priests and didn't dare hit it.
chat.meaning: Visoba had taught him there's no place without God. So Namdev sees Vitthal in the dog, and only worries the bread is dry.

ghee.meaning: clarified butter, used in Indian cooking and offerings

Aundha.meaning: the temple town where tradition places the turning temple

Guru Granth Sahib.meaning: the scripture of the Sikhs, which keeps some of Namdev's hymns

Vitthal.meaning: the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur

Namdev.meaning: the tailor's son who became a poet-saint of Pandharpur

notes: All paraphrase; nothing quoted. The dog-and-ghee story is hagiography, framed as 'the story told about him'; confirm the telling, including the variant where Vitthal appears.

The turning-temple hymn: confirm the raag and Ang (now given as Raag Malar, Ang 1292) and that the paraphrase is fair ('laughing and playing', seized and driven out, the reference to his birth community, the temple turning). A Sikh reviewer may also want to check the line about his hymns sitting beside the Gurus'.
Aundha (Aundha Nagnath) as the temple is placed with 'tradition places it'; the hymn itself may not name the place. Confirm.
Caste is handled as 'a man of his birth' and 'the community he was born into'; a Keeper may prefer naming his community (shimpi, tailor and cloth-printer) as the hymn does.
Original left null to avoid repeating yesterday's विठ्ठल.
